UK workplace pension: the band that sets contributions and the route that sets the take-home cost

Separate qualifying earnings from total salary, split the 8% minimum between employee and employer, and compare net pay with relief at source using pounds sterling and the 2026/27 Income Tax bands.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

UK workplace pension: the qualifying-earnings band and two routes to tax relief

Interactive planning lab

Qualifying earnings between the band limits£28,760
Employee contribution before tax relief£1,438
Employer contribution£862.8
Take-home cost after basic-rate relief£1,150.4

Pounds sterling (GBP) throughout; no CAD conversion. Public GOV.UK automatic-enrolment rules checked 25 October 2026: 5% employee and 3% employer minimums on qualifying earnings between £6,240 and £50,270, with 8% combined. Tax relief is modelled at the 20% basic rate up to taxable income of £50,270 and the 40% higher rate above it, using the £12,570 personal allowance stated for the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. Earnings are capped at £100,000 so the personal-allowance taper, additional rate, Scottish rates and Welsh rates remain outside the model. The model holds one annual earnings figure constant, ignores bonuses or irregular pay, and does not determine eligibility, scheme pensionable pay, annual allowance, carry-forward, salary sacrifice, National Insurance, student loan, other deductions, investment return, fees, or the timing of actual payroll and relief payments. Employer contributions are not deducted from the employee’s pay. Net pay means the contribution comes out before Income Tax; relief at source means the employee pays net and the provider claims basic-rate relief. Neither route is assumed to be available in every scheme.

The central idea

Automatic-enrolment contributions apply to earnings between two limits, not to the whole salary. The employee’s gross contribution can be the same under net pay and relief at source, while the take-home cost differs when there is little or no Income Tax to relieve.

01

Start with qualifying earnings, not the salary headline

Automatic enrolment does not normally apply the minimum percentage to every pound of salary. GOV.UK describes most automatic-enrolment schemes as basing contributions on total earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year before tax. Those are the band limits used here. Earnings below the lower limit produce no qualifying earnings in this simplified model. Earnings above the upper limit do not increase the contribution base.

The legal minimum from April 2019 is 3% from the employer and 5% from the employee, for 8% in total. Scheme rules can require more, and a scheme may use a different definition of pensionable pay. The model therefore applies the selected rates to the band, not to gross salary, and states that choice rather than presenting it as every workplace scheme.

Within the band, each additional pound of earnings adds the selected employee percentage and the selected employer percentage. At the defaults, £1 more of qualifying earnings adds 5p to the employee contribution and 3p to the employer contribution. Those are separate cash sources: the employer amount is not deducted from the employee’s pay.

02

Read the default year as three separate amounts

At £35,000 of annual earnings, £28,760 lies between the limits. At 5% and 3%, the employee contribution is £1,438 and the employer contribution is £862.80, for £2,300.80 credited across the year. The employee’s gross contribution is 5% of the band, not 5% of £35,000, and the combined amount is about 6.57% of salary.

Calling £1,438 the “cost” of the pension would mix a gross contribution with a take-home amount. Under net pay, that gross figure is deducted before Income Tax, so the reduction in take-home pay is smaller for a taxpayer. Under relief at source, the employee pays a net amount and the provider adds basic-rate relief. Both routes aim at the same gross contribution, but the cash movements differ.

The employer amount is also not free money in the sense of being available for other spending. It is paid by the employer into the pension instead of being paid as salary in this comparison. The model does not assume that rejecting the pension would raise salary by the same amount.

03

Net pay: the contribution comes out before Income Tax

In a net-pay scheme, the employee contribution is taken from pay before Income Tax is calculated. At the 20% basic rate, £100 of gross contribution reduces take-home pay by about £80, because £20 of Income Tax is no longer due on the amount contributed. The pension still receives the full £100. That is the default equality the model shows for a basic-rate taxpayer with enough taxable income.

At higher rates the relief can be larger. If the contribution is relieved at 40%, £100 of gross contribution reduces take-home pay by about £60. The exact amount depends on where the contribution sits across the tax bands, which is why the model calculates tax with and without the contribution instead of applying a single percentage to the whole amount.

Net pay is not automatically better for everyone. Someone whose income is below the Personal Allowance may pay no Income Tax on the contribution in the first place, so there is no tax to relieve. That case is shown separately, because a scheme using net pay can produce a different take-home result from one using relief at source for the same gross contribution.

04

Relief at source: pay net, and the provider claims basic-rate relief

Under relief at source, the employee pays a net amount from take-home pay and the pension provider claims basic-rate relief from the government and adds it to the pot. At the 20% basic rate, £80 paid by the employee becomes £100 credited. The government top-up is 20% of the gross contribution, or 25% of the net payment.

The GOV.UK guidance states that this at-source relief is available even to someone who does not pay Income Tax, and that a Scottish taxpayer paying 19% still receives a 20% at-source claim without paying the difference. That is why the low-earnings comparison can favour relief at source: the same £100 gross contribution can require less take-home cash.

Higher-rate relief is different. The provider claims the basic 20%, and the additional relief is claimed through Self Assessment. The model treats that extra amount as a separate step that arrives later. If the claim is not made, or is delayed, the eventual take-home cost is higher than the chart’s relief-at-source bar assumes.

05

Compare the routes at low earnings and at higher rates

At £10,000 of earnings, qualifying earnings are £3,760. At 5%, the employee contribution is £188 and the employer contributes £112.80. Because £10,000 is below the £12,570 Personal Allowance, the model calculates no Income Tax to relieve. Net pay therefore reduces take-home pay by the full £188. Relief at source requires £150.40 from take-home pay, and the provider adds £37.60, so the same £188 reaches the pension for £37.60 less current cash.

At £12,570 the gap remains, because there is still no taxable income. Between the Personal Allowance and the point where the employee contribution is fully covered by taxable income, the two routes converge gradually rather than switching at a single salary. At £20,000 and above in the model, a basic-rate taxpayer reaches the same take-home cost under either route.

At £60,000, qualifying earnings are capped at £44,030. The employee contribution is £2,201.50 of the £3,522.40 combined. Net pay reduces take-home pay by about £1,320.90 through 40% relief. Relief at source takes £1,761.20 from pay, adds £440.30 at source, and leaves £440.30 to claim. The final cost can match, but the cash flow does not: one route delivers the relief through payroll, the other through a claim.

06

Do not read the 8% minimum as 8% of salary

The combined contribution of £2,300.80 at £35,000 is about 6.57% of salary because £6,240 of earnings sits below the band. At £60,000 the combined £3,522.40 is about 5.87% of salary because only £44,030 is inside the band. At £8,000, qualifying earnings are £1,760, so the 8% minimum produces £140.80 combined, or about 1.76% of salary.

These percentages describe this band model at the selected rates. They are not the scheme’s contribution rate, a replacement rate, or a statement about retirement income. A scheme using total pay, pensionable pay or a different band would produce a different relationship between salary and contribution.

The flat contribution above the upper limit is also an arithmetic result of the band, not a cap on what an employer or employee may contribute. Additional voluntary contributions, salary sacrifice and scheme-specific rates are outside the model.

07

Keep salary sacrifice, eligibility and investment results outside the comparison

The model does not calculate salary sacrifice. Under salary sacrifice, the employee gives up salary in exchange for an employer pension contribution, which can change National Insurance and the contractual pay figure. It is a different arrangement from either net pay or relief at source and is not treated as equivalent here.

It also does not determine whether a particular worker is eligible for automatic enrolment, what a scheme counts as pensionable pay, whether an employer uses a qualifying scheme, or how much annual allowance is available. Those questions depend on the employment, the scheme and the tax year. The model assumes one steady annual earnings figure and full periods, with no bonus, commission, overtime, sickness, parental leave or partial year.

Scottish and Welsh Income Tax rates, the Personal Allowance taper above £100,000, the additional rate, student loan repayments and other payroll deductions are outside the displayed figures. Investment returns, fund fees, vesting, transfer rules and the tax treatment of withdrawals are also excluded: the charts stop at the contribution credited, not at a retirement balance.

08

Use four questions on a real payslip or scheme statement

First, identify the earnings definition the scheme actually uses. Is the contribution based on the £6,240–£50,270 band, on total pay, or on a scheme-specific pensionable pay figure? The percentage cannot be checked without that base.

Second, identify the relief route. A net-pay scheme should show the contribution reducing taxable pay before Income Tax. A relief-at-source scheme should show a net deduction and a separate provider claim. If the payslip shows only a deduction, the two are easy to confuse.

Third, separate the employee amount from the employer amount. A combined “pension” line can hide which side pays what, and the employer amount should not be subtracted from take-home pay a second time. Fourth, if a higher or additional rate applies, check whether the extra relief needs a Self Assessment claim and whether it has arrived.

A change of job, a pay rise across a band limit, or a move between schemes can change both the contribution base and the relief route. Recheck the band and the method rather than carrying forward last year’s percentage.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. GBP throughout. Public GOV.UK automatic-enrolment and Income Tax rules checked 25 October 2026. Independent example earnings and contribution rates; no payroll record, eligibility determination, return or fee is modelled. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. GOV.UK · Workplace pensions: what you, your employer and the government pay ↗

    Checked 25 October 2026. Used for the automatic-enrolment minimum of 3% employer, 5% employee and 8% total from April 2019, and for the statement that most automatic-enrolment schemes base contributions on total earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year before tax. The page also notes that scheme rules can require more, and that a scheme may define pensionable pay differently; the model applies the band only as a stated simplification.

  2. GOV.UK · Tax on your private pension contributions ↗

    Checked 25 October 2026. Used for the two automatic relief routes: contributions taken from pay before Income Tax, and relief at source where the provider claims basic-rate relief and adds it to the pot. The page states that relief at source still applies to people who do not pay Income Tax, that a Scottish 19% rate still receives a 20% at-source claim, and that higher-rate relief is claimed through Self Assessment.

  3. GOV.UK · Income Tax rates and Personal Allowances ↗

    Checked 25 October 2026. Used for the £12,570 standard Personal Allowance, the 20% basic rate to £50,270, the 40% higher rate above it, and the statement that the current tax year runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The model caps earnings at £100,000 so the Personal Allowance taper and additional rate are not calculated.
